title: Installing an open mesh floor
subtitle: Better ventilation and a passive mite monitor in one fitting.
excerpt: An open mesh floor replaces the solid wooden floor on a national hive with a wire mesh panel. Mites that fall off bees pass through the mesh and cannot return to the colony. A slide-in mite board turns the floor into a passive varroa monitor. Here is how to fit one and how to read the count it gives you.
sourceNotes: NBU Beekeeper's Toolkit (2024), section on varroa monitoring and open mesh floors. BBKA factsheet on varroa management. Understanding Varroa Lifecycle, Homemade education entry.

glossaryTerms.definition: A beehive floor with a wire mesh panel instead of a solid board. Mites and debris fall through the mesh to the ground. Commonly abbreviated OMF in UK beekeeping.
The count of varroa mites that fall off adult bees each day. Collected on a sticky board placed under the open mesh floor, then divided by the number of days the board was in place.

content.text: improves hive ventilation and reduces condensation in winter. Its second job is passive monitoring. With a slide-in mite board in place, the floor counts how many varroa fall naturally each day, giving you an early warning of rising mite pressure without opening the hive.
Choose a calm, mild day. Suit up and smoke the entrance lightly before opening.
Gently ease the brood box off the old solid floor with the hive tool, and slide the new mesh floor into place on the hive stand.
Lower the brood box onto the mesh floor. Check that the entrance block is seated correctly and the entrance is not obstructed.
Slide the varroa mite board into the slot below the mesh from the back of the hive. The board collects debris and fallen mites.
Close the hive and leave for seven days before reading the mite board.

After seven days, slide the board out and count the mites on it. Mites are rounded, brown-red dots, smaller than a sesame seed. Debris from wax and propolis will be present; look for the characteristic shape. Divide the total by seven to get the
0–2 mites per day in spring: low mite load. Monitor monthly.
3–6 per day in early summer: moderate. Plan a Apiguard or oxalic acid treatment after harvest.
7–10+ per day: high. Treat now. Mid-summer varroa counts at this level indicate a colony under serious pressure.

Remove the mite board in winter, or replace it with a solid insert board to reduce cold draughts through the mesh during hard frost. UK winters below -5°C for more than a few days can chill a small colony on an uninsulated mesh floor. A crown board with a layer of insulation above it compensates for most of the heat loss through the open floor.
